newsitem.title: FRANCE: Buses resume in two French towns as strikes weaken.
newsitem.headline: Buses resume in two French towns as strikes weaken.

text.p: Public transport resumed in two cities in France on Tuesday, leaving only a handful of cities gripped by a 13-day stoppage by drivers demanding shorter working hours and early retirement.
Buses got back to normal in the Mediterranean port of Toulon and in the north-eastern city of Lille after drivers accepted a management offer of shorter hours.

In the south-western city of Toulouse, a bastion of the stoppages where drivers have been on strike for 23 days, about half the usual buses were running, staffed by non-striking drivers under police protection for a second day in a row.

About 600 people, including drivers from other cities carrying banners, marched through Toulouse, stopping at city hall, in solidarity with the strikers, police said. Organisers put the figure at 1,000.
The strike continued to hit transport in Cannes, Nice, Le Mans, Clermont-Ferrand and Sete.

The nationwide stoppages, inspired by Toulouse, began 13 days ago in 20 provincial cities with unions seeking a cut in working hours to 35 hours from 39 with no pay cut, and retirement at 55 years rather than at 60.
Transport companies have given ground on working hours but less on early retirement.
The strikes are the latest labour challenge to the centre-right government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, which last year bowed to truckers' demands for retirement at 55 after they blocked roads.
